title: Two Sum
statement: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`. You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. You can return the answer in any order.

examples.explanation: nums[0] + nums[1] = 2 + 7 = 9, which equals target. So we return [0, 1].
nums[1] + nums[2] = 2 + 4 = 6, which equals target. So we return [1, 2].
nums[0] + nums[1] = 3 + 3 = 6, which equals target. So we return [0, 1].

returnRequirement: Return an array of two indices [i, j] such that nums[i] + nums[j] == target.

title: Contains Duplicate
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears at least twice in the array, and `false` if every element is distinct.

examples.explanation: The value 1 appears at indices 0 and 3, so a duplicate exists.
All four values are distinct, so no duplicates exist.
Multiple values such as 1, 3, 4, and 2 each appear more than once.

returnRequirement: Return true if any element appears more than once, otherwise return false.

title: Valid Anagram
statement: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s`, and `false` otherwise. An anagram is a word formed by rearranging the letters of another word using all the original letters exactly once.

examples.explanation: Both strings contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies: a×3, n×1, g×1, r×1, m×1.
"rat" contains {r,a,t} while "car" contains {c,a,r}. The character sets differ, so they are not anagrams.

returnRequirement: Return true if t is an anagram of s (same characters, same frequencies), otherwise return false.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement: You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a given stock on the `i-th` day. You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock. Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If no profit is possible, return `0`.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price = 1) and sell on day 5 (price = 6). Profit = 6 - 1 = 5. Note that buying on day 2 and selling on day 1 is not allowed because you must buy before you sell.
Prices only decrease each day, so no profitable transaction is possible. Return 0.

returnRequirement: Return the maximum profit achievable from a single buy-sell transaction, or 0 if no profit is possible.

title: Majority Element
statement: Given an array `nums` of size `n`, return the majority element. The majority element is the element that appears more than `⌊n / 2⌋` times. You may assume that the majority element always exists in the array.

examples.explanation: n = 3, so the majority threshold is ⌊3/2⌋ = 1. The element 3 appears 2 times, which is more than 1.
n = 7, so the majority threshold is ⌊7/2⌋ = 3. The element 2 appears 4 times, which is more than 3.
n = 5, so the majority threshold is ⌊5/2⌋ = 2. The element 1 appears 3 times, which is more than 2.
n = 3, so the majority threshold is ⌊3/2⌋ = 1. The element 5 appears 2 times, which is more than 1.

returnRequirement: Return the element that appears more than ⌊n/2⌋ times in the array.

title: Move Zeroes
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, move all `0`'s to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements. Note that you must do this in-place without making a copy of the array.

examples.explanation: The non-zero elements [1, 3, 12] are moved to the front in their original relative order, and the zeros are pushed to the end.
There is only one element which is 0. The array remains unchanged.

returnRequirement: Modify nums in-place so all zeros are moved to the end while preserving the relative order of non-zero elements. Do not return a new array.

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
statement: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number sorted in non-decreasing order. Note that the array may contain negative numbers whose squares could be larger than those of positive numbers.

examples.explanation: Squaring each element gives [16, 1, 0, 9, 100]. Sorting in non-decreasing order yields [0, 1, 9, 16, 100].
Squaring each element gives [49, 9, 4, 9, 121]. Sorting in non-decreasing order yields [4, 9, 9, 49, 121].

returnRequirement: Return a new array containing the squares of each element from nums, sorted in non-decreasing order.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
statement: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, remove the duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears only once. The relative order of the elements should be kept the same. Return `k`, the number of unique elements. The first `k` elements of `nums` must contain the unique elements in their original order. The remaining elements beyond the first `k` do not matter.

examples.explanation: The two unique elements are [1, 2]. The function returns k = 2, and the first 2 elements of nums are modified to [1, 2].
The five unique elements are [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]. The function returns k = 5, and the first 5 elements of nums are modified accordingly.

returnRequirement: Return k, the count of unique elements. The first k elements of nums must hold the unique values in their original order.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays
statement: Given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, return an array of their intersection. Each element in the result must be unique, and you may return the result in any order.

examples.explanation: The only element present in both arrays is 2. Even though 2 appears multiple times in both arrays, it is included only once in the result.

returnRequirement: Return an array of unique elements that appear in both nums1 and nums2.

title: Merge Sorted Array
statement: You are given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, sorted in non-decreasing order, and two integers `m` and `n` representing the number of elements in `nums1` and `nums2` respectively. Merge `nums2` into `nums1` as one sorted array in-place. `nums1` has a total length of `m + n`, where the last `n` elements are set to `0` as placeholder space.

examples.explanation: Merging [1,2,3] and [2,5,6] into a single sorted array gives [1,2,2,3,5,6]. The result is stored in-place in nums1.

returnRequirement: Do not return a value. Modify nums1 in-place so its first m+n elements form a sorted merged array.

title: 3Sum
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, return all the triplets `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` such that `i != j`, `i != k`, `j != k`, and `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`. The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.

examples.explanation: nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2] = -1 + 0 + 1 = 0. nums[1] + nums[2] + nums[4] = 0 + 1 + (-1) = 0. nums[0] + nums[3] + nums[4] = -1 + 2 + (-1) = 0. The distinct triplets are [-1,-1,2] and [-1,0,1].

returnRequirement: Return a list of all unique triplets [a, b, c] such that a + b + c == 0, with no duplicate triplets.

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is equal to the product of all the elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`. You must solve it in O(n) time without using the division operation.
returnRequirement: Return an array where each element at index i is the product of all elements in nums except nums[i].

title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane)
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum = 4 + (-1) + 2 + 1 = 6.

returnRequirement: Return the largest sum of any contiguous subarray within nums.

title: Container With Most Water
statement: You are given an integer array `height` of length `n`. There are `n` vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the `i-th` line are `(i, 0)` and `(i, height[i])`. Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container that holds the most water. Return the maximum amount of water the container can store. You may not slant the container.

examples.explanation: Lines at index 1 (height 8) and index 8 (height 7) form the optimal container. Width = 8 - 1 = 7, effective height = min(8,7) = 7, so water = 7 * 7 = 49.

returnRequirement: Return the maximum volume of water that can be contained between any two lines.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
statement: Given a string `s`, return the longest palindromic substring in `s`. A palindrome is a string that reads the same forwards and backwards. If there are multiple answers of the same length, return any one of them.

examples.explanation: Both "bab" (centered at index 1) and "aba" (centered at index 2) are valid palindromic substrings of length 3. Either is acceptable.

returnRequirement: Return the longest palindromic substring within s. If multiple substrings of equal maximum length exist, return any one.

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Given an array of strings `strs`, group the strings that are anagrams of each other. You can return the answer in any order. Two strings are anagrams if one can be formed by rearranging the letters of the other.

examples.explanation: "eat", "tea", and "ate" are all anagrams of each other. "tan" and "nat" are anagrams of each other. "bat" has no anagram partner in the list.

returnRequirement: Return a list of groups, where each group contains strings that are anagrams of one another.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order. It is guaranteed that the answer is unique.
constraints: k is in range [1, number of unique elements]

examples.explanation: Element 1 appears 3 times, element 2 appears 2 times, and element 3 appears once. The 2 most frequent elements are 1 and 2.

returnRequirement: Return an array of the k elements with the highest occurrence frequency in nums.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
statement: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `k`, return the total number of contiguous subarrays whose elements sum to exactly `k`.

examples.explanation: There are two subarrays that sum to 2: nums[0..1] = [1,1] and nums[1..2] = [1,1].

returnRequirement: Return the total count of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k.

title: 4Sum
statement: Given an array `nums` of `n` integers and an integer `target`, return all unique quadruplets `[nums[a], nums[b], nums[c], nums[d]]` such that `a`, `b`, `c`, and `d` are all distinct indices and `nums[a] + nums[b] + nums[c] + nums[d] == target`. The solution set must not contain duplicate quadruplets.

examples.explanation: -2+(-1)+1+2=0, -2+0+0+2=0, and -1+0+0+1=0 are all the unique quadruplets summing to 0.

returnRequirement: Return a list of all unique quadruplets [a, b, c, d] such that a + b + c + d == target.

title: Rotate Array
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, rotate the array to the right by `k` steps, where `k` is non-negative. A right rotation by one step moves the last element to the front of the array.

examples.explanation: Rotating right by 1: [7,1,2,3,4,5,6]. Rotating right by 2: [6,7,1,2,3,4,5]. Rotating right by 3: [5,6,7,1,2,3,4].

returnRequirement: Modify nums in-place so it is rotated to the right by k steps.

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: You are climbing a staircase with `n` steps to reach the top. Each time you can either climb `1` or `2` steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?

examples.explanation: There are two ways to climb 2 steps: (1 step + 1 step) or (2 steps).

returnRequirement: Return the number of distinct ways to climb to the top of n stairs.

title: Fibonacci Number
statement: The Fibonacci sequence is defined as: `F(0) = 0`, `F(1) = 1`, and `F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2)` for `n > 1`. Given `n`, return `F(n)`.
returnRequirement: Return the n-th Fibonacci number.

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
statement: You are given an integer array `cost` where `cost[i]` is the cost of the `i-th` step on a staircase. Once you pay the cost, you can either climb one or two steps. You can start from index `0` or index `1`. Return the minimum cost to reach the top of the floor (beyond the last step).

examples.explanation: Start at index 1 (cost 15), then jump two steps to the top. Total cost = 15.

returnRequirement: Return the minimum total cost to reach the top of the staircase.

title: Maximum Subarray
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum, and return its sum.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum = 4 + (-1) + 2 + 1 = 6.

returnRequirement: Return the largest sum of any contiguous subarray.

title: House Robber
statement: You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed. Adjacent houses have interconnected security systems — if two adjacent houses are broken into on the same night, the police will be alerted. Given an integer array `nums` representing the amount of money in each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob without alerting the police.

examples.explanation: Rob house 1 (money = 1) and then rob house 3 (money = 3). Total = 1 + 3 = 4.

returnRequirement: Return the maximum amount of money that can be robbed without robbing two adjacent houses.

title: Pascal's Triangle
statement: Given an integer `numRows`, return the first `numRows` of Pascal's triangle. In Pascal's triangle, each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it. The triangle starts with a single `1` at the top, and each row begins and ends with `1`.
returnRequirement: Return a list of lists representing the first numRows rows of Pascal's triangle.

title: Divisor Game
statement: Alice and Bob take turns playing a game, with Alice going first. There is a number `n` on a chalkboard. On each player's turn, they must choose a number `x` such that `1 <= x < n` and `n % x == 0`, then replace `n` with `n - x`. A player who cannot make a move loses. Return `true` if Alice wins assuming both players play optimally.

examples.explanation: Alice chooses x = 1 (since 2 % 1 == 0), reducing n to 1. Bob cannot make a move (no x satisfies 1 <= x < 1), so Bob loses and Alice wins.

returnRequirement: Return true if Alice wins with optimal play, otherwise return false.

title: Is Subsequence
statement: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `s` is a subsequence of `t`, or `false` otherwise. A subsequence is a sequence that can be derived from another string by deleting some or no characters without changing the order of the remaining characters.

examples.explanation: We can find 'a' at index 0, 'b' at index 2, and 'c' at index 5 in t, all in order. So "abc" is a subsequence of "ahbgdc".

returnRequirement: Return true if all characters of s appear in t in the same relative order, otherwise return false.

title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, implement a data structure that efficiently handles multiple range sum queries. Each query asks for the sum of the elements between indices `left` and `right` (inclusive). Design a solution that preprocesses the array so that each query can be answered in O(1) time.

examples.explanation: The sum of elements at indices 0 to 2 is: nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2] = -2 + 0 + 3 = 1.

returnRequirement: Return the sum of nums[left] + nums[left+1] + ... + nums[right] for each query.

title: Counting Bits
statement: Given an integer `n`, return an array `ans` of length `n + 1` such that for each `i` (`0 <= i <= n`), `ans[i]` is the number of `1`'s in the binary representation of `i`.

examples.explanation: 0 in binary is 0 → zero 1-bits. 1 in binary is 1 → one 1-bit. 2 in binary is 10 → one 1-bit.

returnRequirement: Return an array of length n+1 where each element at index i contains the number of 1-bits in the binary representation of i.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement: Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their longest common subsequence. A common subsequence is a subsequence that appears in both strings. If there is no common subsequence, return `0`.

examples.explanation: The longest common subsequence is "ace", which has length 3.

returnRequirement: Return the length of the longest subsequence present in both text1 and text2.

title: Coin Change
statement: You are given an integer array `coins` representing coins of different denominations and an integer `amount` representing a total amount of money. Return the fewest number of coins needed to make up that amount. If that amount cannot be made up by any combination of the coins, return `-1`. You may assume you have an unlimited supply of each coin denomination.

examples.explanation: 11 = 5 + 5 + 1, using 3 coins. No combination uses fewer coins.

returnRequirement: Return the minimum number of coins needed to make up the given amount, or -1 if it is not possible.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. A subsequence is derived from the array by deleting some or no elements without changing the order of the remaining elements.

examples.explanation: The longest strictly increasing subsequence is [2,3,7,101] or [2,5,7,101], both of length 4.

returnRequirement: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence in nums.

title: Word Break
statement: Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more words from `wordDict`. Note that the same word in the dictionary may be reused multiple times.

examples.explanation: "leetcode" can be split as "leet" + "code", both of which are in wordDict.

returnRequirement: Return true if s can be fully segmented using words from wordDict, otherwise return false.

title: Unique Paths
statement: There is a robot on an `m x n` grid. The robot starts at the top-left corner and wants to reach the bottom-right corner. The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time. How many unique paths are there from the top-left to the bottom-right?

examples.explanation: On a 3x7 grid, there are exactly 28 distinct paths from the top-left to the bottom-right when only moving right or down.

returnRequirement: Return the number of unique paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner of an m x n grid.

title: Edit Distance
statement: Given two strings `word1` and `word2`, return the minimum number of operations required to convert `word1` to `word2`. The allowed operations are: Insert a character, Delete a character, or Replace a character.

examples.explanation: horse → rorse (replace 'h' with 'r') → rose (delete 'r') → ros (delete 'e'). That's 3 operations.

returnRequirement: Return the minimum number of single-character insert, delete, or replace operations to transform word1 into word2.

title: Decode Ways
statement: A message containing letters from A-Z is encoded using the mapping 'A' → "1", 'B' → "2", ..., 'Z' → "26". Given a string `s` containing only digits, return the total number of ways to decode it. Note that a leading zero (e.g., "06") is not a valid encoding.

examples.explanation: "12" can be decoded as "AB" (1, 2) or "L" (12). There are 2 ways.

returnRequirement: Return the total number of distinct ways to decode the digit string s.

title: Palindromic Substrings
statement: Given a string `s`, return the number of palindromic substrings in it. A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string. A string is palindromic if it reads the same forward and backward. Single characters are always palindromes.

examples.explanation: The three palindromic substrings are "a", "b", and "c". Each single character is a palindrome.

returnRequirement: Return the total count of palindromic substrings in s.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, find a contiguous subarray that has the largest product and return that product. Note that negative numbers can flip the sign of the running product, so both the maximum and minimum product at each position must be tracked.

examples.explanation: The subarray [2,3] has the largest product = 2 * 3 = 6. Including -2 or 4 would not increase the product.

returnRequirement: Return the largest product of any contiguous subarray.

title: Target Sum
statement: You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`. Assign either a `+` or `-` sign to each element in `nums`, then sum all the signed values. Return the number of different assignments that result in a total equal to `target`.
returnRequirement: Return the number of distinct sign assignments to elements of nums that produce a sum equal to target.

title: Invert Binary Tree
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree (mirror it), and return its root. Inverting a binary tree means swapping the left and right children of every node.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100].

examples.explanation: The left and right children of every node are swapped. Node 4's children swap from (2,7) to (7,2), node 7's children swap from (6,9) to (9,6), and node 2's children swap from (1,3) to (3,1).

returnRequirement: Return the root of the inverted binary tree.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth. The maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 10^4].

examples.explanation: The longest root-to-leaf path is 3 → 20 → 15 (or 3 → 20 → 7), which passes through 3 nodes.

returnRequirement: Return the maximum depth of the binary tree as an integer.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of the diameter of the tree. The diameter is the length of the longest path between any two nodes in the tree, measured in number of edges. This path may or may not pass through the root.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].

examples.explanation: The longest path is [4,2,1,3] or [5,2,1,3], each passing through 3 edges.

returnRequirement: Return the number of edges in the longest path between any two nodes in the tree.

title: Balanced Binary Tree
statement: Given a binary tree, determine if it is height-balanced. A height-balanced binary tree is one in which the left and right subtrees of every node differ in height by no more than one.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 5000].

examples.explanation: The left subtree of root (node 9) has depth 1, and the right subtree (node 20) has depth 2. The difference is 1, and all subtrees similarly satisfy the balance condition.

returnRequirement: Return true if the tree is height-balanced (every node's subtrees differ in depth by at most 1), otherwise return false.

title: Same Tree
statement: Given the roots of two binary trees `p` and `q`, check if they are structurally identical with the same node values. Two binary trees are the same if they have the same shape and every corresponding node has the same value.
constraints: The number of nodes in both trees is in the range [0, 100].

examples.explanation: Both trees have the root value 1, left child value 2, and right child value 3. The structure and all values match.

returnRequirement: Return true if both trees have the same structure and identical node values at every position, otherwise return false.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values as a list of lists. Each inner list contains the values of all nodes at that depth level, from left to right.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 2000].

examples.explanation: Level 0 contains only the root: [3]. Level 1 contains nodes 9 and 20: [9,20]. Level 2 contains nodes 15 and 7: [15,7].

returnRequirement: Return a list of lists, where each inner list contains node values at that level from left to right.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
statement: Given a binary tree and two nodes `p` and `q`, find their lowest common ancestor (LCA). The LCA is defined as the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` as descendants (a node can be a descendant of itself).
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [2, 10^5].

examples.explanation: Node 5 is in the left subtree and node 1 is in the right subtree of root 3. The deepest node that is an ancestor of both is the root 3.

returnRequirement: Return the node that is the lowest common ancestor of p and q.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on the right side of it. Return the values of the nodes that are visible from the right side, ordered from top to bottom. The rightmost node at each depth level is the one visible.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100].

examples.explanation: Level 0: only node 1 is visible → 1. Level 1: nodes 2 and 3 exist; the rightmost is 3. Level 2: nodes 5 and 4 exist; the rightmost is 4.

returnRequirement: Return a list of values of the rightmost node at each depth level, from top to bottom.

title: Number of Islands
statement: Given an `m x n` 2D binary grid representing a map where `'1'` represents land and `'0'` represents water, return the number of islands. An island is a group of adjacent land cells connected horizontally or vertically, surrounded by water or the grid boundary.

examples.explanation: All the connected land cells form a single island. There are no separate groups of land cells.

returnRequirement: Return the total number of distinct islands in the grid.

title: Course Schedule
statement: There are `numCourses` courses labeled from `0` to `numCourses - 1`. You are given a list of `prerequisites` where `prerequisites[i] = [a, b]` means you must take course `b` before course `a`. Return `true` if you can finish all courses, or `false` if there is a cyclic dependency that makes it impossible.

examples.explanation: Course 0 must be taken before course 1. There is no cycle, so it is possible to complete both courses.

returnRequirement: Return true if it is possible to finish all courses without a cyclic prerequisite dependency, otherwise return false.

title: Clone Graph
statement: Given a reference to a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy (clone) of the graph. Each node contains a value and a list of its neighbors. The clone must have the same structure and values as the original, but consist of entirely new node objects.
constraints: The number of nodes in the graph is in the range [0, 100].

examples.explanation: The cloned graph has 4 nodes with the same adjacency structure as the input. All neighbor relationships are preserved in the new copy.

returnRequirement: Return the reference to the cloned graph's starting node.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
statement: There is an `m x n` rectangular island that borders the Pacific Ocean on its top and left edges, and the Atlantic Ocean on its bottom and right edges. Rain water can flow from a cell to an adjacent cell (up, down, left, right) only if the adjacent cell's height is less than or equal to the current cell's height. Return a list of grid coordinates where water can flow to both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans.

examples.explanation: Each returned coordinate can reach both oceans by flowing downhill or across equal-height cells.

returnRequirement: Return all [row, col] coordinates from which water can flow to both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans.

title: Rotting Oranges
statement: You are given an `m x n` grid where each cell has one of three values: `0` (empty cell), `1` (fresh orange), or `2` (rotten orange). Every minute, any fresh orange that is 4-directionally adjacent to a rotten orange also becomes rotten. Return the minimum number of minutes until no fresh orange remains. If it is impossible for all oranges to rot, return `-1`.

examples.explanation: Starting from the single rotten orange at (0,0), rot spreads outward each minute. After 4 minutes, all reachable fresh oranges have become rotten.

returnRequirement: Return the minimum number of minutes for all fresh oranges to rot, or -1 if it is impossible.

title: Network Delay Time
statement: You are given a network of `n` nodes labeled from `1` to `n`, and a list `times` of directed edges `times[i] = (u, v, w)` representing a signal traveling from node `u` to node `v` with delay `w`. A signal is sent from source node `k`. Return the minimum time it takes for all `n` nodes to receive the signal. If it is impossible for all nodes to receive the signal, return `-1`.

examples.explanation: Signal sent from node 2 reaches node 1 in time 1 and node 3 in time 1. From node 3, it reaches node 4 in time 1+1=2. The last node to receive the signal is node 4 at time 2.

returnRequirement: Return the time at which the last node receives the signal, or -1 if any node cannot be reached.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
statement: Given the root of a binary search tree (BST) and an integer `k`, return the `k`-th smallest value (1-indexed) among all node values in the tree. Recall that in a BST, all left descendants are smaller than the node, and all right descendants are greater.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is n.

examples.explanation: The in-order traversal of the BST is [1, 2, 3, 4]. The 1st smallest element is 1.

returnRequirement: Return the k-th smallest value in the BST using 1-based indexing.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST). A valid BST requires that for every node: all nodes in its left subtree have values strictly less than the node's value, and all nodes in its right subtree have values strictly greater than the node's value. This property must hold recursively for all subtrees.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].

examples.explanation: Node 2's left child is 1 (1 < 2 ✓) and right child is 3 (3 > 2 ✓). All BST conditions are satisfied.

returnRequirement: Return true if the binary tree satisfies all BST properties, otherwise return false.

title: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node
statement: You are given a perfect binary tree where all leaves are on the same level and every parent has exactly two children. Each node has an additional `next` pointer. Populate each `next` pointer to point to the next right node at the same level. If there is no next right node, set `next` to `null`. Initially, all `next` pointers are set to `null`.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 4096].

examples.explanation: Node 1's next → null (#). Node 2's next → node 3, node 3's next → null. Node 4's next → 5, node 5's next → 6, node 6's next → 7, node 7's next → null.

returnRequirement: Return the root of the tree after all next pointers have been populated.

title: Redundant Connection
statement: You are given a graph that started as a tree with `n` nodes labeled from `1` to `n`, to which one additional edge was added. The graph is represented as an array `edges` where `edges[i] = [a, b]` indicates an undirected edge between nodes `a` and `b`. Return the edge that, when removed, results in a valid tree. If multiple answers exist, return the edge that appears last in the input.

examples.explanation: The first two edges form a valid tree: 1-2 and 1-3. Adding edge [2,3] creates a cycle. Since it is the last edge that causes the cycle, [2,3] is the redundant edge to remove.

returnRequirement: Return the last edge in the input that creates a cycle and can be removed to restore a valid tree.

title: Path Sum III
statement: Given the root of a binary tree and an integer `targetSum`, return the number of paths in the tree where the sum of values along the path equals `targetSum`. The path must go downward (from parent to child) but does not need to start at the root or end at a leaf.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 1000].

examples.explanation: The three paths that sum to 8 are: 5→3, 5→2→1, and -3→11.

returnRequirement: Return the number of downward paths in the tree whose node values sum to targetSum.
